evidence.claim: A shore loop crosses South Cove and passes Fenwick’s golf course.
evidence.quote: It passes by the Fenwick Golf Course just prior to passing over the South Cove.

evidence.claim: The southern loop of Route 154 follows Long Island Sound and crosses South Cove, linking Saybrook Manor, Fenwick and Old Saybrook Center.
evidence.quote: It heads south on Great Hammock Road as it is parallel to the Long Island Sound.

evidence.claim: The southern loop of Route 154 follows Long Island Sound and crosses South Cove, linking Saybrook Manor, Fenwick and Old Saybrook Center.
evidence.quote: It passes by the Fenwick Golf Course just prior to passing over the South Cove.

evidence.claim: The 6.10 miles from Saybrook Manor to the east junction with Old Boston Post Road form a state scenic road.
evidence.quote: The southern loop portion of Route 154 in Old Saybrook, from its beginning at Saybrook Manor (milepost 0.00) to the east junction with Old Boston Post Road in Old Saybrook Center (milepost 6.10) is a state scenic road.

evidence.claim: Fenwick sits where the Connecticut River enters the Sound, separated from the town center by a cove and causeway.
evidence.quote: Fenwick is set off from the town center of Old Saybrook by a large cove crossed by a causeway. It is located exactly where the Connecticut River flows into Long Island Sound

evidence.claim: This loop began its numbered life as State Highway 338 in 1922 and became Route 154 in 1932.
evidence.quote:
At the same time, a loop route in Old Saybrook, serving the borough of Fenwick was designated as State Highway 338.
Route 154 was established in 1932 as a renumbering of old State Highway 338.

evidence.claim: This loop began its numbered life as State Highway 338 in 1922 and became Route 154 in 1932.
evidence.quote: In 1922, the Middlesex Turnpike alignment became part of New England Interstate Route 10 (renumbered to Route 9 in 1932).

evidence.claim: The original route returned from Fenwick along Maple Avenue. In 1935, the western side moved onto Plum Bank Road and Great Hammock Road, establishing the present alignment.
evidence.quote: then continued through Fenwick along Maple Avenue to end at itself just south of the town center. In 1935, a section of Maple Avenue between Summerfield Road and Main Street was redesignated Route 154A and the western part of the loop moved to the current alignment along Plum Bank Road and Great Hammock Road (former SR 603).

evidence.claim: The highway’s role expanded in 1967, when the opening of the Route 9 freeway transferred an old surface-road section to Route 154. That extension ran from US 1 to Essex Road in Old Saybrook, beyond the original shore loop.
evidence.quote: In 1967, with the opening of the Route 9 freeway, the former surface route of Route 9 between US 1 and Essex Road in Old Saybrook was transferred to Route 154.

evidence.claim: From US 1, drive south along Great Hammock Road and Plum Bank Road, then east through Knollwood to Fenwick.
evidence.quote: Route 154 begins at US 1 in Old Saybrook. It heads south on Great Hammock Road as it is parallel to the Long Island Sound. It becomes known as Plum Bank Road, shortly before turning eastward as Indianola Drive as it enters Knollwood. Maple Avenue turns on to Route 154 as it enters Fenwick.

evidence.claim: The road passes the golf course and crosses South Cove before turning sharply west onto College Street.
evidence.quote: It passes by the Fenwick Golf Course just prior to passing over the South Cove. It becomes Bridge Street for a short time before executing a sharp turn to the west as College Street, and later Main Street.

evidence.claim: Main Street then turns north beside North Cove toward the loop’s end at Old Boston Post Road.
evidence.quote: Route 154 soon turns north, passing just to the west of North Cove.

evidence.claim: Main Street then turns north beside North Cove toward the loop’s end at Old Boston Post Road.
evidence.quote: to the east junction with Old Boston Post Road in Old Saybrook Center (milepost 6.10) is a state scenic road.

evidence.claim: Shingle-style houses give Fenwick’s historic district much of its architectural character.
evidence.quote: Architecturally, the Fenwick Historic District is composed largely of Shingle-style residences

evidence.claim: Seventeen of its 60 main buildings represent that style, with others in Queen Anne and Victorian styles.
evidence.quote: Of the district's 60 main buildings, 17 represent examples of the Shingle style, with some others in Queen Anne or Victorian styles.

evidence.claim: Look for flared eaves, upper floors extending beyond the walls below, and small roofs over doors and windows.
evidence.quote: Other frequently observed common architectural features include flares at the eaves of roofs, upper stories that overhang lower stories, and pent roofs over windows and doors.

evidence.claim: The golf course took shape from empty lots in the late 1800s. Its nine holes have been rearranged several times, most recently in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: In the late 1800s The Fenwick Golf Course was created from several empty lots in the center of the district

evidence.claim: Its nine holes have been rearranged several times, most recently in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: The 9-hole golf course has changed layouts on several occasions, with the most recent re-design in the 1930s

evidence.claim: St. Mary’s-By-the-Sea, built in 1883, shares the district’s flared eaves and overhanging forms.
evidence.quote: All of the three are typified in St. Mary's-By-the-Sea, a 1 and 1/2 story church building at 30 Agawam Avenue, designed by Francis Goodwin and built in 1883.

evidence.claim: Most of Fenwick falls within the historic district, which entered the National Register in 1995.
evidence.quote: Most of the borough is included in the Fenwick Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: which entered the National Register in 1995.
evidence.quote: was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1995.

evidence.claim: Two lights mark the harbor channel at the Connecticut River’s mouth: Lynde Point’s Inner Light and the Saybrook Breakwater Outer Light.
evidence.quote: The two lighthouses mark the harbor channel at the mouth of the Connecticut River.

evidence.claim: Two lights mark the harbor channel at the Connecticut River’s mouth: Lynde Point’s Inner Light and the Saybrook Breakwater Outer Light.
evidence.quote: The lighthouse is also known simply as "Breakwater Light" or "Outer Light". It is one of two built off Lynde Point in the nineteenth century. The other lighthouse, known as Lynde Point Light or more commonly as "Inner Light"

evidence.claim: The Inner Light began as a 35-foot wooden tower completed in 1803.
evidence.quote: The first light was a 35 feet (11 m) wooden tower constructed by Abisha Woodward for $2,200 and it was completed in 1803.

evidence.claim: Sailors found the original tower too short to see effectively, a problem worsened by fog from the marshland. It was replaced
evidence.quote: The light was criticized by many sailors for being too short to be seen at an effective distance, a problem exacerbated by a local fog from the marshland that obscured the light.

evidence.claim: It was replaced by a 65-foot octagonal brownstone tower, built in 1838 and first lit in 1839.
evidence.quote: A new 65-foot (20 m) octagonal brownstone tower was constructed in 1838 and lit in 1839.

evidence.claim: Painted white, the replacement has six windows, all facing the water.
evidence.quote: The lighthouse is painted white and has six windows, all facing the water.

evidence.claim: The sparkplug-shaped Outer Light appears on Connecticut’s Preserve the Sound license plates.
evidence.quote:
Saybrook Breakwater Lighthouse is a sparkplug lighthouse in Connecticut,
United States, at Fenwick Point at the mouth of the Connecticut River near Old Saybrook, Connecticut. It is featured on the state's "Preserve the Sound" license plates.

evidence.claim: The Inner Light’s six windows all face the water.

evidence.claim: At Saybrook Point, railroad remains occupy part of the site of Fort Saybrook.
evidence.quote: The rail facilities are built partly on the archaeological remains of Fort Saybrook, the main fortification of the 17th-century Saybrook Colony

evidence.claim: The Connecticut Valley Railroad began service between the point and Hartford in 1871, the year it built its roundhouse and turntable here.
evidence.quote: The Connecticut Valley Railroad was chartered in 1868, and began operations three years later, providing service between Saybrook Point and Hartford

evidence.claim: the year it built its roundhouse and turntable here.
evidence.quote: The roundhouse and turntable were built in 1871 by the Connecticut Valley Railroad

evidence.claim: The extension to the point closed in 1922, and the facilities were abandoned.
evidence.quote: The extension to Saybrook Point ceased operations in 1922, and its facilities were abandoned.

evidence.claim: Excavations in 1981–82 exposed the surviving remains. In Fort Saybrook Monument Park, portions of the roundhouse’s brick-and-stone foundations and the turntable’s concrete base are exposed, with signs explaining their use.
evidence.quote: The exposed facilities were excavated in 1981-2.

evidence.claim: In Fort Saybrook Monument Park
evidence.quote: located in Fort Saybrook Monument Park off Main Street in Old Saybrook, Connecticut.

evidence.claim: portions of the roundhouse’s brick-and-stone foundations and the turntable’s concrete base are exposed, with signs explaining their use.
evidence.quote: The roundhouse was a quarter-round structure housing six bays, with foundations of brick and stone, supporting both the structure and the tracks on which the railroad cars ran.  The turntable had a concrete base.  Portions of these features are exposed in the park, with interpretive signage explaining the use and history of the site.

evidence.claim: The wider railroad complex once included an icehouse, coal bin, steamboat dock, depot and signal tower; the roundhouse and turntable are its only surviving remnant.
evidence.quote: are the only surviving remnant of what was once a large facility, with an icehouse, coal bin, steamboat dock, depot, and signal tower.
